findings.who: A filer whose prior-year AOC was questioned in an IRS letter or exam. The filer agreed to the change, didn't respond so the credit was removed by default, or filed an amended return taking the credit off after the IRS asked for documents.
findings.why_no: They read 'Has the IRS ever denied or reduced' as a contested IRS decision. They see an agreed adjustment, a default for not responding, or their own withdrawal as something they did, not a denial by the IRS.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 1: "If your American opportunity credit was denied or reduced for any reason other than a math or clerical error for any tax year beginning after 2015, you must attach a completed Form 8862"
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count it as denied or reduced even if you agreed to the change, didn't answer an IRS letter, or removed the credit on an amended return after IRS contact.'

findings.who: A filer whose AOC was cut by an IRS notice after a missing or mismatched Form 1098-T, an EIN problem, or a 4-year limit problem. The filer can't tell whether this counts as a 'math or clerical error'.
findings.why_no: The exclusion 'for more than a math or clerical error' asks for a legal classification. A filer who thinks any automated notice was a math or clerical fix answers No.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 1: "denied or reduced for any reason other than a math or clerical error for any tax year beginning after 2015"
findings.fix: First ask whether the IRS ever removed or lowered an AOC claimed by you or your spouse for 2016 or later, for any reason. On Yes, ask whether the notice said the change was a math or clerical error, and treat any other or unknown reason as needing Form 8862.

findings.who: A filer whose final determination of reckless disregard or fraud came recently, after an older claim. A 2-year or 10-year ban may still be running.
findings.why_no: The help says 'Count only a denial or reduction for 2016 or a later year.' A filer may apply that limit to the bar too, look at the year of the determination or the original claim, and decide it falls outside the window.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3: "Don’t claim the American opportunity credit for 2 years after there was a final determination that your claim was due to reckless or intentional disregard of the rules or 10 years after there was a final determination that your claim was due to fraud."
findings.fix: Make clear that the 2016 limit refers to the tax year of the claim, and that a bar counts as long as its 2-year or 10-year period, measured from the final determination, hasn't ended.
